takeaways: Where content is organized into sections, section headings mark them.
Level AAA. It applies to sections of writing, such as articles, help pages and long documents, not to UI components like buttons or cards.
Headings let people jump to the part they need and see the shape of a long text before reading it.
Related rules: whether headings are marked up in code is 1.3.1; whether they describe their content is 2.4.6. This one asks that the headings are there at all.
failures: A long help article with no headings, only paragraphs
Sections set apart by spacing or a divider line alone
Bold lead-in sentences standing in for headings
check: Scroll a long page in the file. Where does the topic change, and is there a heading there?
Read only the headings. Do they show the structure of the content?
Check that the content templates in the system let writers add headings.

quiz.question: A policy page is one long block of text split into topics with extra white space. What does 2.4.10 ask for?
options: Add a heading at the start of each topic
Add more white space between topics
Put each topic in a collapsible accordion
quiz.why: The rule asks for section headings where content is organized into sections. White space shows a break but does not name it, and an accordion still needs headings for its sections.

spec: Mark each section heading and its level in long content templates.
Note which visual styles are real headings and which are just large text.
Give writers guidance on when a section needs a heading.
review: Could I find the part I need by reading only the headings?
Is this bold line a heading or just styled text?
Does the template let writers add headings, or does it squeeze everything into one block?
tradeoff: Headings add length and can make short content feel bureaucratic. Short pieces with one topic do not need them; any page people scan or come back to should have them. Meeting this AAA rule is usually cheap and worth it.
system: Build content templates and rich text components with heading styles mapped to heading levels, so writers can structure content without custom styling.
pitch: Nobody reads a wall of text. Headings make our content findable for everyone and cost nothing but a little editing.
